meta.title: Scienteens Lab · From Mersenne to Kundt
meta.description: An interview workshop that follows the history and physics of sound from Mersenne's measurements to Kundt's tube.

hero.title: Making sound visible.
hero.introduction: A five-part workshop that begins with an early measurement of the speed of sound and ends by measuring a standing wave inside a Kundt tube.

interview.title: From Mersenne to Kundt
interview.summary: The workshop follows one question: how can we move from hearing sound to observing and measuring it?

facts.label: Central question
facts.value: What is sound—and how can we see it?

steps.title: Measuring the speed of sound
paragraphs: In Harmonie universelle (1636), Marin Mersenne reported an early quantitative attempt to measure the speed of sound. He used gunfire over a known distance and compared the visible flash with the delayed report.
His result was not very accurate, but the method established a powerful idea: if sound covers a known distance in a measured time, its speed can be calculated.

steps.title: We know its speed—but what is sound?
paragraphs: Measuring a speed does not yet tell us what is moving. This question was already discussed in antiquity. In De Anima, Aristotle connected sound with impact and with motion transmitted through the surrounding air.
This becomes the central problem of the workshop: what travels from the source to the listener when the air itself does not travel across the room?

media.title: The speed of sound depends on the medium
media.caption: The disturbance covers the same distance at different rates in steel, water and air. This observation motivates the next question: what property of the medium controls the propagation?

source.label: Aristotle, De Anima, Book II, Chapter 8

steps.title: From a pulse to a standing wave
paragraphs: A Slinky and a particle model build the wave concept in four steps: local motion creates a travelling disturbance, periodic motion introduces frequency and wavelength, a transverse representation makes the geometry visible, and superposition with a reflected wave produces a standing pattern.

substeps.title: A travelling pulse
substeps.text: I send a longitudinal impulse through a Slinky. Each coil only oscillates around its equilibrium position, while the compression travels from one coil to the next. This separates the motion of matter from the propagation of energy and information.

media.alt: Animation of a hand creating a longitudinal pulse in a horizontal spring.
media.title: Matter moves locally; the pulse travels
media.caption: The hand moves parallel to the spring. A compression propagates to the right although the coils remain near their equilibrium positions.

substeps.title: Sound propagation, wavelength and frequency
substeps.text: How can a local disturbance set neighbouring regions in motion? When a loudspeaker moves forward, it compresses the air immediately in front of it. The resulting pressure differences accelerate neighbouring regions, which change the pressure and density farther along. When the loudspeaker moves back, it creates a rarefaction. These local changes are transmitted through the air as a longitudinal sound wave.
paragraphs: The Slinky makes this mechanism visible: deforming one section changes the elastic forces acting on neighbouring sections and sets them in motion. Each section has inertia, so its response takes time. In air, elasticity is associated with resistance to compression. The medium's elastic properties and mass density help determine the propagation speed. The acoustic motion remains local while the disturbance travels through the medium.

In research presented in 1748 and published in 1750, Leonhard Euler analysed interactions between neighbouring parts of an elastic medium under a disturbance and extended the model to many parts. His work provides a historical route from local interactions to the propagation of a sound wave.

A periodic source repeats the disturbance at a frequency f, measured in oscillations per second. In the resulting periodic wave, the wavelength λ is the distance between two successive compressions, or between two successive rarefactions. During one period T = 1 / f, the wave advances by one wavelength: λ = vT. Therefore, v = λ / T = fλ.

For sound in air under the same conditions, the propagation speed is approximately independent of frequency over the audible range. Increasing the frequency then shortens the wavelength. In the Kundt tube, a known driving frequency and a measured wavelength will allow us to determine the speed of sound.

source.label: François Baskevitch, Calculer la vitesse du son après Newton : le défi du jeune Euler, p. 45

media.alt: Animation of a loudspeaker producing successive compressions in air molecules.
media.title: A periodic disturbance in air
media.caption: The air molecules oscillate locally. The compression pattern moves away from the loudspeaker; the spacing between successive compressions represents one wavelength.

media.alt: Animation comparing several periodic patterns with different spatial repetitions.
media.title: Different wavelengths in the same medium
media.caption: The coloured patterns advance through the same medium. A pattern with more repetitions over the same distance has a shorter wavelength and therefore a higher frequency; fewer repetitions mean a longer wavelength and a lower frequency, because v = fλ.

substeps.title: A transverse representation
substeps.text: I then drive the Slinky transversely so that amplitude and wavelength are easier to see. The coils move perpendicular to the direction of propagation. Sound in air remains longitudinal: the sinusoidal curve is a representation of displacement as a function of position, not the trajectory followed by an air molecule.

media.alt: Diagram comparing compressions in a longitudinal wave with the sinusoidal representation of a transverse wave.
media.title: Longitudinal and transverse waves
media.caption: Particles oscillate parallel to propagation in a longitudinal wave and perpendicular to it in a transverse wave. Both descriptions use the same wavelength, frequency and propagation speed.

media.alt: Diagram showing wavelength measured horizontally between two equivalent points of a transverse wave.
media.title: Measuring wavelength on a transverse wave
media.caption: One wavelength is the horizontal distance between two consecutive crests—or any two points in the same phase. The particles oscillate vertically while the pattern propagates horizontally.

substeps.title: Reflection, superposition and standing modes
substeps.text: A wave sent along the Slinky reflects at the end. The incoming and reflected waves overlap, and their displacements add: y = y₁ + y₂. At selected driving frequencies, the boundary conditions are satisfied and a stable pattern of nodes and antinodes appears. In a tube closed at both ends, the ends impose displacement nodes and the allowed modes satisfy L = nλ / 2. The filmed demonstration will compare several of these standing modes.

media.alt: Two snapshots of a standing sine wave sharing the same fixed red nodes.
media.title: Fixed nodes, oscillating antinodes
media.caption: The red nodes remain at zero displacement while the sections between them oscillate. This temporary diagram will be complemented by the filmed sequence of standing modes.

steps.title: From Chladni figures to a closed tube
paragraphs: In 1787, Ernst Chladni showed how sand on a vibrating plate traces nodal lines. The plate and the air column are different systems, but the visual idea is the same: a standing vibration can leave a spatial pattern.

In an ideal tube closed at both ends, air displacement is zero at each end. Only wavelengths that satisfy the boundary conditions can form standing modes; pressure antinodes occur where the displacement nodes are located.

media.alt: Historical line drawing of a vibrating plate sprinkled with sand and excited with a bow.
media.title: Making nodal lines visible
media.caption: As the plate vibrates, grains leave the strongly moving regions and collect along nodal lines. Chladni figures turn an invisible standing vibration into a visible spatial pattern.

source.label: E. F. F. Chladni, Entdeckungen über die Theorie des Klanges (1787)

steps.title: A wavelength written in dust
paragraphs: In 1866, August Kundt published a method based on acoustic dust figures inside a tube. The repeated pattern reveals the spacing d between adjacent nodes: half a wavelength.
Measure d, double it to obtain λ, then combine the wavelength with the known driving frequency f. The visible pattern becomes a measurement of the speed of sound.
The real power of the experiment is comparison. By filling the tube with different gases and repeating the measurement, the speed of sound in each gas can be determined.

media.title: Kundt tube experiment
media.caption: The final experiment video will be added here.

source.label: August Kundt, On a New Kind of Acoustic Dust Figures (1866)
